title: The face grows bright
hook: in the company of the holy the face grows bright and filth is washed

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seventh salok: God beyond reach, and the wondrous story of the holy. Your line was good company. Did you send that message? Today, the first stanza of ashtpadi seven. Day four hundred sixty-three.

There's an old saying in many languages: tell me who your friends are, and I'll tell you who you are. Parents say a version of it to teenagers. Coaches say it to athletes. Researchers keep finding versions of it, too: people around us shape what we eat, how we spend, even how we feel. We soak up the people we sit with. Guru Arjan says it more than four hundred years ago, and says it as good news. The first stanza of ashtpadi seven begins with a face that changes.
screen: `TELL ME WHO YOUR FRIENDS ARE.` → `WE SOAK UP WHO WE SIT WITH.` → `A FACE THAT CHANGES.`

segments.voice: Today's word is saadh sangat. Saadh, you met yesterday: a holy person. Sangat is company, gathering, the people you're with. Put together: the company of the holy. In Sikh life the word sangat on its own came to mean the congregation, the people sitting together before the Guru Granth Sahib. The stanza opens with two lines. Saadh kai sang mukh oojal hot: in the company of the holy, the face becomes bright. Oojal is bright, clean, radiant. In Punjabi, a bright face is also a way of talking about honor: the opposite of a face blackened with shame. So the line means both: you look lighter, and you can hold your head up. Then: saadhsang mal sagalee khot. In the holy company, all the filth is washed off. Mal is dirt, grime, the kind that builds up without your noticing. Neither line says the holy company scrubs you. It's quieter than that. You sit with good people and some of their brightness rubs off on your face. You spend time where the Name is sung, and the grime you didn't know you were carrying starts to loosen. Company shapes you. The stanza doesn't say this is a matter of rules or effort. It says it the way you'd describe sunlight: sit in it and you warm up. That's why, for Sikhs, going to the sangat matters, not just reading alone. The company is part of the medicine.
screen: `SAADH: HOLY. SANGAT: COMPANY.` · `OOJAL: THE FACE GROWS BRIGHT.` · `MAL: THE GRIME WASHES OFF.` · `LIKE SITTING IN SUNLIGHT.` · then, large: `COMPANY SHAPES YOU.`

segments.voice: The practice is to spend time with someone good today: a call, a walk, a meal, even ten minutes. For now, prepare for it. Picture who that could be. Then sit and imagine you're already beside them. Let your face relax, the forehead, the eyes, the mouth, the way a face does in good company. Notice that relaxing is something your face already knows how to do. If you pray, you can ask to be good company for someone else too. The bell holds the time.
Saadh sangat. The company of the holy, where, the stanza says, the face grows bright and the grime washes off.
Your line: company shapes you. Today, spend time with one good person on purpose, and afterward notice your own face. Day four hundred sixty-three.

screen: `DAY 463 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EGO LEAVES IN GOOD COMPANY.`

howItsDone: Sikhs speak of the sangat, the congregation gathered before the Guru Granth Sahib, as the saadh sangat, and many make a point of joining it regularly rather than practicing only alone.

original.note: Gurmukhi: saadh sangat, the company of the holy; for Sikhs, the gathered congregation.

trapdoor: what you thought: holy company is a nice extra to private devotion.
what it means: the stanza says company itself changes you: the face grows bright, grime washes off.
what a scholar hears: 'mukh oojal' is idiomatic for honor (as 'kaalaa mukh' is for disgrace); 'sangat' became the standard Sikh term for the congregation.
